item.title: Binance Reports $6.3 Billion Crypto Heist Executed in 20 Minutes by Alleged North Korean Hackers
item.description: Cryptocurrency exchange Binance has reported a massive security breach resulting in the theft of approximately $6.3 billion in digital assets across multiple blockchains. The attack, which occurred on October 29, 2026, involved hackers draining funds from Binance wallets within a 20-minute window, according to analysis by crypto tracing firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis. Binance immediately suspended deposits and withdrawals while investigating the incident, and has managed to freeze about half of the stolen funds, primarily stablecoins. However, the remaining $3.3 billion, mostly in Bitcoin, Ether, and XRP, cannot be frozen and may be irrecoverable. Multiple crypto tracing firms, including Elliptic, TRM Labs, and Chainalysis, have linked the attack to North Korean hacking group TraderTraitor, known for sophisticated crypto heists. item.title: Prescription Eye Drops Offer Temporary Relief for Presbyopia, But Not a Complete Replacement for Reading Glasses
item.description: Prescription eye drops such as Vizz and Yuvezzi, approved by the FDA in 2025 and 2026 respectively, aim to treat presbyopia, the age-related condition that makes it difficult to focus on close objects. These drops work by shrinking the pupils, creating a pinhole effect that improves near vision. However, the benefits are temporary, lasting up to 10 hours for Vizz and eight for Yuvezzi, after which users must rely on reading glasses again. The drops can help users read smaller text without enlarging the font, potentially improving near vision from 20/60 to 20/30, but results vary based on individual vision, print size, and lighting conditions. Side effects include reduced night vision, headaches, and potential risks like retinal tears, which necessitate a pre-treatment eye exam. Cost is also a factor, with Vizz priced at $79 for 25 doses and Yuvezzi at $79 for 30 days. item.title: Congo's Ebola Outbreak Claims Over 5,000 Lives Amid Containment Challenges
item.description: The Democratic Republic of Congo's ongoing Ebola outbreak has surpassed 5,000 deaths, with 5,026 fatalities out of 10,351 confirmed cases, according to the Congolese Ministry of Health. The Bundibugyo virus strain, declared in mid-May, has become the second deadliest Ebola outbreak in history, trailing only the 2014-2016 West Africa epidemic that killed 11,000 people. Health officials report a nearly 50% lethality rate, with 2,788 recoveries. The outbreak has spread to 67 of Congo's 178 health zones across eight provinces, with Ituri and North Kivu emerging as epicenters. The eastern region, where the virus is concentrated, faces significant challenges including armed conflict involving the M23 rebel group and Islamist insurgencies, which limit healthcare access. Community distrust has led to attacks on health workers, including the killing of a nurse responding to an Ebola alert. item.title: Mercedes-Benz T80: The Unfinished Land Speed Record Attempt from 1939
item.description: The Mercedes-Benz T80, a six-wheeled land speed record vehicle developed in 1939, was designed to achieve speeds exceeding 600 km/h (373 mph) but never completed an official run due to the outbreak of World War II. Conceived by racing driver Hans Stuck and engineered by Dr. Ferdinand Porsche under the sponsorship of Daimler-Benz, the project aimed to showcase German technological prowess under Adolf Hitler's regime. The T80 featured a massive 44.5-liter DB 603 aircraft engine, capable of producing 3,000 horsepower, and was built at a cost of approximately 600,000 Reichsmarks (around $5 million today). The vehicle's design included innovative features such as a hydraulic torque converter, mechanical anti-spin control, and a special fuel mixture to prevent engine detonation. Standing 8.1 meters long and weighing nearly 3,000 kilograms, the T80 was intended to break the land speed record on a 10-kilometer stretch of the Dessau Autobahn in January 1940. item.title: Yvonne Furneaux: A Graceful Presence in Mid-Century European Cinema
item.description: Yvonne Furneaux (1926–2024) was a British-French actress renowned for her refined beauty and significant contributions to mid-century European cinema. Born Elisabeth Yvonne Scatcherd in Roubaix, France, to English parents, she received her education at Oxford and the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art before embarking on her film career in the early 1950s. Furneaux collaborated with esteemed directors such as Michelangelo Antonioni, Federico Fellini, and Roman Polanski, appearing in notable films including Le Amiche (1955), La Dolce Vita (1960), and Repulsion (1965). Her versatility allowed her to excel in both art-house and genre films, bringing a distinctive elegance and quiet intensity to her roles. With her dark features and sophisticated presence, Furneaux became one of the most graceful faces of 1950s and 1960s European cinema. item.title: Scientists Explore Theoretical Possibility of Black Hole Fragmentation
item.description: Black holes are known for colliding and merging, producing gravitational waves, but the idea of a black hole splitting into two has been considered highly improbable due to their immense gravitational pull. However, a recent study by European scientists explores the theoretical possibility of black hole fragmentation under specific conditions. The research, led by Francesco Sannino from the University of Naples Federico II and the University of Southern Denmark, along with colleagues Giacomo Cacciapaglia, Manuel Del Piano, and Vania Vellucci, examines how a rapidly rotating black hole might fragment into two separate entities. The team's calculations suggest that if a black hole rotates close to its maximum possible rate, it could theoretically split, forming what they describe as a 'pair-of-pants topology'—where the event horizon takes on a shape resembling two legs of a pair of pants. item.title: Pingualuit Crater: A Natural Wonder with the Purest Water on Earth
item.description: The Pingualuit Crater, located in the remote Arctic region of Quebec, Canada, is renowned for containing the purest water found in nature. Discovered in 1943 by a U.S. military reconnaissance flight, the crater is a nearly perfect circle measuring three kilometers in diameter, filled with water that has no external sources of inflow or outflow. The lake's purity stems from its unique hydrological system: water enters only through precipitation and leaves solely through evaporation, resulting in extremely low salinity levels—hundreds of times lower than those found in rivers or the Great Lakes. This makes Pingualuit one of the most transparent lakes on the planet. The crater, formed approximately 1.5 million years ago by an asteroid impact, is one of the best-preserved impact craters on Earth, with minimal erosion due to successive glaciations. item.title: Packers Edge Panthers 27-19 Despite Special Teams Errors and Late Comeback Threat
item.description: The Green Bay Packers secured a narrow 27-19 victory over the Carolina Panthers on Thursday Night Football, overcoming multiple challenges to improve their record to 5-3. The game featured several critical moments that defined the outcome. The Packers struggled with special teams issues, including a missed extra point and two fumbles, while allowing the Panthers to mount a significant comeback attempt after trailing 27-10 midway through the third quarter. Carolina outgained Green Bay 109-32 in the fourth quarter, but the Packers held on to win. Christian Watson, a key receiver, left the game in an ambulance after sustaining a chest injury in the first half but returned to play a crucial role in the final minutes, catching a 7-yard reception on third-and-2 with 2:33 remaining to help run down the clock. The Panthers' quarterback Bryce Young completed 23-of-41 passes for 209 yards with a touchdown and an interception, but was sacked six times, including four by rookie Dani Dennis-Sutton.

item.title: Crocodiles' Climate Preference Explains Survival After Dinosaur-Killing Asteroid Impact
item.description: Scientists from University College London have uncovered a key factor in why crocodiles survived the asteroid impact that wiped out the dinosaurs 66 million years ago. Their research, published in Science Advances, reveals that crocodiles' long-standing preference for warm environments placed them in tropical refuges that remained habitable even after the catastrophic event. The study analyzed over 7,000 fossils and climate data from 400 species spanning 245 million years. Researchers found that while dinosaurs' habitats contracted severely following the impact, crocodile relatives maintained access to suitable tropical regions near the equator. These areas provided critical refuges where populations could persist and eventually recover. item.description: In the final days of April 1945, as Soviet forces advanced into Berlin, Adolf Hitler and Eva Braun died by suicide in the Führerbunker, a reinforced concrete shelter beneath the Reich Chancellery. He believes that the desire for local AI computing—where individuals run models on their own devices—is misguided, as it leads to inefficient use of scarce resources. item.title: Antarctic Ocean Currents Reverse Abruptly, Threatening Global Climate Systems
item.description: An international study published in Nature Climate Change reveals a significant shift in Antarctic ocean currents, with the Antarctic Intermediate Water (AAIW) experiencing a rapid reversal in salinity, density, and depth since 2016. The research, led by the University of Melbourne and the Indian Institute of Science, found that declining Antarctic sea ice has abruptly reduced seasonal meltwater delivery, causing the AAIW layer to become warmer, saltier, denser, and deeper within less than a decade. For two decades prior to 2016, the AAIW was replenished with freshwater from seasonal Antarctic sea ice melt, with annual meltwater volumes equivalent to three times the Amazon River's flow. However, after 2016, sea ice decline led to a one-third reduction in freshwater input, triggering rapid salinification and densification. Shatner also expressed condolences to Stewart's wife Sunny and family. item.title: Families desperate for news as rescuers work to identify Spanish train crash victims
item.description: Spain is holding three days of mourning after a train collision south of Madrid on Wednesday, October 28, which killed 69 people and injured 112. Rescue efforts continue as emergency workers search through wreckage to identify victims and locate missing individuals. The Spanish civil guard has deployed over 900 personnel from specialized departments. Among the deceased is former Employment Minister Fátima Báñez, 59, who was traveling on the train. King Felipe VI visited a hospital in Toledo to express condolences to victims' families and thank rescue workers. Relatives of missing passengers are using social media to share details about their loved ones, including seat numbers and photos, in hopes of finding information. Leaked audio recordings reveal that a high-speed train was given clearance to move despite another train being stalled ahead, suggesting systemic failures in railway management. item.title: Federal Judge Rejects DOJ's Demand to Remove 20,000 Ballots in California Election
item.description: U.S. District Judge David O. Carter, a Clinton appointee and former Marine who earned a Bronze Star and Purple Heart in Vietnam, has rejected the Trump administration's request for California to set aside over 20,000 ballots cast by voters the federal government suspects may not be citizens. The judge's ruling, described as 'epic' by former U.S. Attorney Joyce Vance, directly challenges the Justice Department's authority, stating that the federal government cannot coerce states to abandon their constitutional election procedures. Carter emphasized that 'California and its people are sovereign, too,' and criticized the government's lack of transparency regarding the methodology used to identify the voters in question. The Department of Justice had sued California on October 15, minutes after a 48-hour deadline to review a list of over 20,000 voters it labeled 'likely noncitizens.' Jamie Raskin (D-MD), the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, has issued a strong warning that Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump's son-in-law, is 'unfit to serve in any capacity' in government. The report claims these funds were used for illicit purposes, including bribery of a U.S. official and funding war crimes. item.title: Obama's Cheesecake Factory jab exposes Trump's misplaced priorities in White House renovations
item.description: The article discusses a political exchange between former President Barack Obama and current President Donald Trump, centered around a humorous remark made by Obama about Trump's White House renovations. Obama quipped that the White House now looks 'like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory,' referencing Trump's lavish redecorations including a granite helipad, oversized ballroom, and gold leafing. The author, a former PR and political professional, analyzes how Trump's over-the-top response to this joke—defending his renovations in detail and even sending Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to pose outside a Cheesecake Factory—backfired spectacularly. The article highlights how Trump's fixation on defending his 'gold-plated' White House aesthetic while ignoring economic struggles of ordinary Americans created a PR disaster. item.description: According to a report by 404 Media, Proton's CEO Andy Yen is aggressively promoting the adoption of artificial intelligence within the company, while employees describe a work environment characterized by fear that discourages raising security concerns or challenging leadership. The investigation, based on interviews with nine current and former employees, internal Slack chats, meeting recordings, and an AI manifesto from the company's CTO, reveals a culture where engineers are pressured to prioritize AI-driven development over traditional security practices. One employee quoted in the report stated that Yen dismissed security testing requests as 'bullshit and loser thinking,' emphasizing that 'perception is more important than truth' when communicating product features. item.title: Patrick Stewart's Death Linked to Alzheimer's and Lewy Body Dementia, Expert Explains
item.description: British actor Patrick Stewart, known for his iconic roles in 'Star Trek: The Next Generation' and the 'X-Men' franchise, died at age 86 on Wednesday, October 29, 2026. His spokesperson confirmed that he passed away from Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia, conditions that often co-occur. UCLA neurology professor Dr. Keith Vossel explained that when these two conditions are present together, the individual's decline may be faster compared to having just one of the conditions. Lewy body dementia is the second-most-common form of degenerative dementia, following Alzheimer's disease, and occurs when a protein called alpha-synuclein aggregates in clumps inside the brain. The condition is frequently under-recognized and under-diagnosed because its symptoms overlap with those of Alzheimer's. item.title: Anna Carin Bjorck: Swedish Model Who Defined Mid-Century Fashion Elegance
item.description: Anna Carin Bjorck was a Swedish fashion model who gained prominence in the late 1950s and early 1960s. Known for her refined Nordic beauty and graceful presence, she appeared in major American fashion magazines, particularly Vogue, where she was photographed by renowned photographers such as John Rawlings, Irving Penn, and Karen Radkai. Bjorck modeled elegant ready-to-wear and couture looks, often posing with classic American cars of the era, embodying the sophisticated style of mid-century fashion. Her career included appearances in Vogue and Harper's Bazaar, featuring various designers and styles from the period. She was photographed in a variety of elegant outfits, including silk dresses, tailored suits, and evening gowns, often styled with accessories from prominent designers like Dior and Hattie Carnegie. item.description: Waymo has announced a partnership with Toyota to begin testing autonomous Toyota bZ4X vehicles in Japan next year, as part of a broader collaboration to provide electric vehicles for robotaxi operations in international markets, including the U.K. Under the agreement, Toyota will manufacture the 2027 bZ4X vehicles and integrate Waymo's self-driving system at its Takaoka factory in Japan. The electric vehicle, currently known as the BZ in North America, will initially undergo testing in Japan before potentially expanding to other right-hand driving countries like the U.K., where Waymo has been testing its autonomous Jaguar I-Pace vehicles in London for months. The partnership, which follows an 18-month preliminary agreement between the two companies, appears to be more of a conventional vehicle supplier deal that helps Waymo meet regional needs while adding a new model to its robotaxi fleet. item.title: Tyler Perry Challenges Accuser's Disclosure of Private Messages in Sexual Assault Lawsuit
item.description: Tyler Perry is engaged in a legal dispute with Mario Rodriguez, his accuser in a sexual assault case, over the disclosure of private text messages. According to court documents obtained by TMZ, Perry claims he provided private texts with associates to Rodriguez as part of the legal proceedings, but maintained that these communications were intended to remain confidential, as previously agreed. Perry argues that the messages, which include discussions about financial matters, should not be made public because they involve third parties unrelated to the case. The lawsuit, which Rodriguez filed for $77 million, alleges that Perry sexually assaulted him during a 2018 visit to his home. item.title: California Adopts Controversial Water Management Plan for Delta Ecosystem
item.description: California regulators have adopted a controversial plan that significantly alters how the state governs water pumping in the Sacramento-San Joaquin River Delta, the heart of the state's water system. The new approach, endorsed by Governor Gavin Newsom and supported by water agencies serving farms and cities, replaces the traditional requirement for all water agencies to limit pumping to maintain minimum river flows with voluntary agreements. These agreements commit agencies to ensuring specific river flows for environmental protection and funding habitat restoration projects for fish. The State Water Resources Control Board voted 4-1 to approve the plan, with Board Chair E. Joaquin Esquivel calling it a 'modernized regulatory approach' and a 'generational shift' in water management. item.title: The Hardest Places on Earth to Reach, and How to Get There
item.description: The article discusses some of the most remote and difficult-to-reach places on Earth, including Tristan da Cunha, Pitcairn Island, Hang Son Doong, the Ennedi Plateau, Mount Roraima, and Oymyakon. Tristan da Cunha, located in the South Atlantic, is considered the hardest inhabited place to reach, with no airstrip and the nearest city 2,810 kilometers away in Cape Town, requiring a six-day sea voyage. Pitcairn Island is accessed by flying to Tahiti, then taking a weekly flight to Mangareva, followed by a 32-hour sail on the supply ship Silver Supporter. Hang Son Doong, the world's largest cave, can be visited with Oxalis Adventure on a six-day expedition after a fitness test. The Ennedi Plateau in Chad is closed for travel due to safety concerns, with US and UK advising against all travel to the area. item.title: An AI App Predicts Life Expectancy Using Health Data and Biomarkers
item.description: The article details the author's experience with Death Clock, an AI-powered longevity app that predicts life expectancy based on medical habits and lifestyle. The app, launched in 2024, uses data from health questionnaires, biomarker panels, and longevity studies to generate personalized prevention plans. After subscribing to the $69 basic blood panel and adding a stress test for $29, the author received a prediction of their death date at age 74, with causes including cardiovascular disease, sleep disorders, or cancer. The app updated the predicted death age to 73 after noting a family history of diabetes. The author reflects on their growing awareness of aging following the loss of family members and daily physical discomforts, while questioning the app's accuracy and the broader longevity industry's claims. item.title: Solar power growth accelerates as global capacity doubles every three years
item.description: Dr. Simon Clark, a climate communicator with a PhD in atmospheric physics, has declared that global solar power has reached a 'positive tipping point,' with solar capacity now doubling every three years. In a TikTok explainer, Clark cited an S-curve graphic from the WWF's Living Planet Report 2026 to illustrate how the energy transition is moving beyond experimental stages into mainstream adoption. He outlined three stages of the shift: enabling, accelerating, and stabilizing. Clark emphasized that the world's energy system produces three-quarters of greenhouse gas emissions, making the transition critical. He provided examples such as the UK phasing out coal power, Norway's 96% electric vehicle sales for new cars, and India's growing electric two- and three-wheeler market for urban transport. item.title: Prime Minister's inner circle obstructed Treasurer's fiscal proposals ahead of budget
item.description: The article discusses a conflict within the Australian government regarding fiscal policy ahead of the May budget. Treasurer Jim Chalmers reportedly faced obstruction from Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's inner circle, referred to as the 'razor gang,' in implementing cost-saving measures. According to high-level government sources, Chalmers consistently advocated for the lowest-cost options when budget proposals were reviewed by the cabinet's expenditure subcommittee. Budget proposals typically present multiple cost options, allowing ministers to choose between higher or lower spending levels. The obstruction by Albanese's team has intensified scrutiny on the Prime Minister's economic management, as the Labor government scrambles to find savings to offset new spending initiatives. item.title: Attorney General Blanche signs misdemeanor charges in Nevada voter fraud case, raising concerns
item.description: Attorney General Todd Blanche has taken an unprecedented step by personally signing misdemeanor charges against four individuals in Nevada, a move that has drawn significant scrutiny from legal experts. The charges, filed against Adam Klasfeld of All Rise News reported, are part of the Trump administration's ongoing effort to support discredited voter fraud claims in a key swing state. Federal prosecutors had previously brought cases against four people, using them as evidence to counter Nevada officials' findings that a list of 185 individuals, which the federal government claimed were noncitizens, were all U.S. citizens. The Department of Homeland Security had initially alleged that nearly 16,000 noncitizens were on Nevada's voter rolls, but this claim collapsed when state officials reviewed the list. item.title: German Actress Elke Sommer, 1960s Hollywood Icon, Dies at 85
item.description: German actress Elke Sommer, renowned as a 1960s Hollywood icon who starred in films such as A Shot in the Dark and The Prize, has died at the age of 85. She passed away from heart failure on Wednesday night, October 28, 2026, at her residence in the Bel Air neighborhood of Los Angeles. Her stepson, Sebastian Walther, confirmed her peaceful passing, following the July 2026 death of her husband, Wolf Walther. Sommer's career began in 1959 when she was discovered in Italy while vacationing with her mother in Viareggio. A local beauty pageant win and a newspaper photo caught the attention of Italian director Vittorio De Sica, who cast her in the comedy Men and Noblemen. She also made her film debut in The Friend of the Jaguar. To better suit international audiences, she adopted the stage name Elke Sommer, replacing her German surname Schletz. item.title: United Launch Alliance prepares Vulcan rocket for return-to-flight mission on November 13
item.description: United Launch Alliance (ULA) announced on Wednesday that it plans to return its Vulcan rocket to service on November 13, nine months after a solid rocket booster anomaly disrupted the company's 2026 launch schedule. The return-to-flight mission will deploy 40 satellites for Amazon's Leo broadband constellation, marking the first of 38 Vulcan flights contracted by Amazon to build its network. The launch, scheduled to take place from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, remains pending range approval. This mission is critical for ULA following two nozzle failures in the solid rocket boosters during the first four missions of the Vulcan rocket, most recently in February. Although the rocket successfully completed missions despite the failures, U.S. Space Force officials, ULA's primary customer, lost confidence in the Vulcan's reliability. item.title: Polymarket and Binance Experience Security Incidents Involving Third-Party Providers and Internal Transfers
item.description: After a series of security incidents involving Polymarket and Binance, the crypto industry faced a significant test of its infrastructure. Polymarket, a prediction market platform valued at $21 billion, halted trading on its international site after a third-party vendor, DebugBear, was compromised. Users reported drained wallets, and the platform quickly restored trading within an hour. Polymarket confirmed it would fully reimburse affected traders, though details on the number of users impacted and the reimbursement process remain unclear. Meanwhile, Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, experienced significant outflows from its wallets, with stablecoin issuers freezing over $2 billion. Security firm Blockaid suggested the activity could be an internal transfer rather than theft, as one account was set up to allow a designated operator to drain assets. item.title: CNN Analyst Highlights Unprecedented Polling Shifts in Key Senate Races
item.description: Harry Enten, CNN's chief data analyst, expressed astonishment at recent polling data showing Democratic candidates leading in traditionally Republican Senate races in Texas and Kansas. During an appearance on 'The Source with Kaitlan Collins,' Enten described the numbers as 'bonkers' and 'nuts,' noting that Democrats are ahead in Texas by six points with James Talarico and that Kansas, a state that hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, shows a tight race with Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton at 49 percent. Enten emphasized that these polls represent the strongest Democratic showing in Texas since 1988 and in Kansas since at least 1996, suggesting a potential shift in the political landscape of these long-standing Republican strongholds. The analysis highlights a significant change in voter sentiment, with Democrats gaining ground in states that President Trump won in 2024, including Michigan and Texas, while races in Maine and Kansas remain competitive. item.description: A former federal prosecutor, Harry Litman, has warned that the Trump Justice Department's recent legal maneuvering over a taxpayer windfall is heading toward an unavoidable conflict with Congress. Litman, a former U.S. attorney, argued in a Thursday episode of 'Talking Feds' that the DOJ's new brief to the 11th Circuit Court of Appeals hinges on the deal being a genuine settlement, which the department cannot prove. Instead of fighting the case, the DOJ agreed to a voluntary dismissal, a $1.776 billion fund, and a promise to shield Trump from IRS audits of his past taxes. item.description: Economic analyst Catherine Rampell, writing for The Bulwark, argues that corporations that actively collaborated with former President Donald Trump are now experiencing significant anxiety as Democrats appear likely to regain control of at least one chamber of Congress. This development brings with it the potential for congressional subpoenas and investigations into companies that worked closely with the Trump administration. Rampell cites recent reports from The Washington Post and The Wall Street Journal indicating that Democrats are compiling lists of entities—including defense technology firms, military suppliers, and major tech companies—to investigate. item.description: A bipartisan group of 28 former governors from both parties has filed a legal brief with the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals, leveraging former Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell's own words to oppose the Trump Justice Department's lawsuit against California's ballot-counting practices. The governors' brief, filed in support of California and immigrant rights advocates, argues that the federal government's attempt to stop the counting of thousands of ballots constitutes a 'brazenly unlawful and dangerous effort' to usurp state authority over elections. The brief cites McConnell's April 2025 Wall Street Journal op-ed, in which he stated that elections 'may have national consequences but the power to conduct them rests in state capitols,' and emphasized that 'the delegation of authority over election administration is crystal clear.' item.description: Macklemore, the American rapper known for hits like 'Thrift Shop' and 'Same Love,' described his opening night of the Free Palestine tour in Dublin as 'one of the most beautiful moments' of his life, with tears in his eyes throughout the sold-out performance at Dublin's 3Arena on October 26, 2026. The concert, which featured Irish artists Hozier, Kneecap, and actor Liam Cunningham, followed Macklemore's removal from Ed Sheeran's Loop Tour due to his pro-Palestine comments. item.title: Cold Temperatures Activate Muscle-Driven Pathway to Boost Longevity, Study Reveals
item.description: A groundbreaking study published in Nature has uncovered a molecular mechanism by which cold temperatures extend lifespan. Researchers from the University of Cologne identified that mild cold exposure triggers muscle cells to produce dihydrobiopterin (BH2), a metabolite that travels throughout the body to maintain protein homeostasis and support tissue health during aging. The study, conducted on nematode worms (C. elegans) and human cells, reveals that cold temperatures increase production of an enzyme called CAT-4 in muscles, which stimulates BH2 synthesis. This metabolite is then converted into tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4), enabling an enzyme to produce tyrosine, an amino acid critical for cellular function. Disrupting this pathway reduced lifespan benefits in cold-exposed worms, indicating that cold-induced longevity isn't merely a passive metabolic slowdown but an active biological process. item.title: Trump reportedly angered by former attorney Alina Habba's $50 million deal with Venezuelan family
item.description: According to The New York Times, President Donald Trump privately 'erupted' in anger after learning that Alina Habba, a former personal attorney, had secured a lucrative contract with a Venezuelan billionaire family worth over $50 million. The deal, which includes $10 million annually plus bonuses for a four-year term, was reportedly discussed by Trump with aides and allies, who stated he was 'angered' by the amount Habba would earn. Trump reportedly urged Habba to donate part of the funds to his presidential library or another entity bearing his name, and even suggested the Venezuelan family halt further payments. item.description: President Donald Trump has faced criticism for canceling in-person campaign rallies and replacing them with tele-rallies during the midterm election season. According to CBS News White House reporter Jennifer Jacobs, Trump canceled a Sunday rally in Dubuque, Iowa, and a Saturday event in Salina, Kansas, both of which were intended to bolster support for Republican candidates. item.title: Nostalgic 1950s and 1960s Halloween Costumes Capture Childhood Traditions
item.description: These mid-century photographs from the 1950s and 1960s showcase children dressed in Halloween costumes, reflecting the era's simpler, often handmade fashion. The images depict kids in a variety of outfits, including ghosts, witches, pirates, clowns, skeletons, and popular characters of the time, posing proudly before heading out for trick-or-treating or Halloween parties. Many of the costumes were crafted at home, showcasing the creativity and charm of the period. The photos offer a warm, nostalgic glimpse into childhood Halloween celebrations more than half a century ago, highlighting how traditions and styles have evolved over time. The collection provides a visual narrative of community and family traditions during a time when Halloween was celebrated with a focus on handmade decorations and costumes rather than commercialized themes. These images serve as a historical snapshot of how children engaged with the holiday, emphasizing the importance of personal creativity and community

item.title: Deputy Chief of Staff Accused of Extortion and Court Influence Scheme Linked to Custody Battle
item.description: A lawsuit filed in the Southern District of New York has accused Rafi Silberberg, Deputy Chief of Staff to Rep. Mike Lawler (R-NY), along with two other individuals, of orchestrating an extortion and 'court-fixing' scheme targeting Shmuel Goldenberg. According to the complaint, the trio allegedly conspired to influence the outcome of a contentious custody battle involving Goldenberg, demanding extreme measures including the surrender of his home and over $300,000 in child support payments. The lawsuit also alleges that a $50,000 bribe was to be paid directly to Justice Sherri L. Eisenpress, a Rockland County judge who resigned earlier this year following a misconduct investigation. The investigation revealed that Eisenpress had presided over more than 50 cases where she had personal connections to the attorneys involved. item.title: NUS Develops First Touchscreen-Integrated Garment with Washable, Flexible Display
item.description: Researchers at the National University of Singapore's College of Design and Engineering have created the world's first touchscreen integrated into a garment. The innovative technology involves threading a fiber that functions as both pixels and touch sensors, allowing the garment to display images and video, respond to touch, and connect wirelessly to digital devices. The sleeve prototype, featuring 54 pixel fibers each containing 96 LEDs, forms a 96 by 54-pixel display measuring 168 mm by 105 mm with 8-bit color depth and 30 frames per second refresh rate. This groundbreaking development overcomes previous limitations of textile-based displays by using a novel interconnection architecture and thermal fiber drawing process that integrates thousands of microelectronic devices along a single fiber. The display remains washable, breathable, and flexible after 50 detergent washes and 1,000 bends around a 5 mm radius, maintaining nearly identical light output and touch response. The technol

item.description: President Donald Trump confronted a Reuters reporter on Thursday afternoon after the journalist questioned why he was canceling some of his rallies for battleground Senate races in red states. Trump's response was aggressive, calling the reporter 'a sick guy' and criticizing his physical appearance, stating, 'Look at this guy. You’re way out of shape. You are disgusting! Put yourself in shape! You look like hell.' The president's outburst quickly drew mockery and criticism on social media. Commenters highlighted the irony of Trump's remarks given his own public image, with one user noting, 'Trump telling someone they look like hell while standing there looking like a microwaved pumpkin is absolutely hilarious.' Another political strategist observed, 'Trump is fat. He’s sweating. His tanner is running down his face. And literally can’t take the easiest softball question.' item.description: CNN anchor Jake Tapper delivered a sarcastic commentary following President Donald Trump's heated exchange with a reporter regarding his decision to cancel a campaign event in Kansas. The incident occurred after Trump was questioned about abandoning plans to hold a rally with Republican Senator Roger Marshall, who is competing in a challenging reelection campaign. When pressed about his health, Trump responded with an aggressive remark, telling the reporter, 'You are disgusting. Put yourself in shape. You look like hell.' Tapper, upon replaying the footage in the CNN studio, quipped, 'Classy as always,' and added, 'There should be a reverse-angle camera so I know who he’s talking about.' item.description:
Historian Heather Cox Richardson argues in her latest 'Letters from an American' newsletter that the MAGA movement is showing signs of weakening domestically. She cites several recent developments to support her analysis. Richardson also reports on The Independent's findings that Trump merchandise stores are closing nationwide, with one owner stating the store had 'run its course.'
The historian highlights instances of Republicans backing Democratic candidates, including Texas Democrat James Talarico's campaign airing ads featuring five former GOP officials urging votes for him over Republican Ken Paxton. item.description: Simba SC coach Steve Barker has addressed the challenges posed by the CAF Champions League group stage, particularly focusing on the threat presented by Cameroonian newcomers Colombe Sportive. While acknowledging the established names in the group, Barker emphasized that every team presents unique challenges, and Simba must navigate these obstacles to fulfill their continental ambitions this season. item.description: The article details a concerning development involving FBI agents who have reportedly expressed fears that they may be ordered to illegally seize voting machines or ballots in the upcoming election, potentially violating federal law. The agents are particularly worried about the 1865 law that prohibits federal officials from entering polling places armed, which carries penalties of up to five years in prison and a lifetime ban from federal employment. This concern stems from recent actions by the Trump administration, including a raid on Georgia election offices in January 2023, which was conducted under the direction of Tulsi Gabbard, then Director of National Intelligence, and based on claims from election denier Kurt Olsen. item.description: A top aide to U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro was recorded admitting a significant error in a case involving former FBI officials Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, who were charged with lying to Congress about their knowledge of an investigation into Hunter Biden's laptop. The incident came to light during a court hearing where FBI agent Bryan Witt testified about a phone call between Pirro's office and House Judiciary Committee counsel Steve Castor. During the call, Carlton Davis, a special counsel in Pirro's office, reportedly said, 'this is our f--- up,' according to Witt's testimony. The case originated from a directive by Kash Patel, a former Trump administration official, who instructed the FBI to examine certain individuals, including Floris, following President Trump's public accusations against 'rogue bureaucrats' for allegedly hiding information about Chinese election interference. item.title: Federal Judge's Critique Highlights DOJ Credibility Crisis Amid Trump Administration
item.description: A federal judge's sharp criticism of the Justice Department's handling of a dispute over the East Potomac Golf Course has sparked concern among legal experts about the department's credibility. U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued a pointed opinion questioning the Department of Justice's (DOJ) conflicting statements regarding the closure of the golf course, which directly contradicted President Donald Trump's public announcement of a November 15 closure date. The judge's inquiry, 'So who do I believe? Do I believe the President of the United States, or do I believe you?', underscored the growing tension between the executive branch and the judiciary. Former federal prosecutor Harry Litman, writing in his Substack 'Talking Feds,' described Judge Reyes's opinion as a 'frontal attack on the credibility of the entire Department of Justice.' item.title: Jezebel removes over 100 articles with explicit headlines, sparking backlash from former employees
item.description: Jezebel, a women-focused website that launched in 2007 and became known for its edgy and often transgressive feminist content, has removed more than 100 articles from its website. The articles, many of which had sexually explicit or vulgar headlines, now display '404 error' messages. According to a Washington Post review, the publisher stated that the articles were not deleted but temporarily unpublished. The move has caused significant outrage among former staff members, who expressed frustration over the removal of content that was part of the site's identity. The website, which has been a staple of feminist internet culture for nearly two decades, has faced criticism for its decision to take down articles that featured bold and provocative headlines. The publisher's explanation that the content was temporarily unpublished rather than permanently deleted has not quelled the backlash. item.description: President Donald Trump received a high-level military briefing on Thursday as his administration evaluates the possibility of launching another major military campaign against Iran, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal. Admiral Brad Cooper, the top U.S. commander in the Middle East, made a rare in-person visit to the White House to discuss potential military operations, joining Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Joint Chiefs Chairman General Dan Caine. The meeting, which also addressed other topics, occurred as the U.S. weighs 'resuming major combat operations,' the Journal reported. item.description: President Donald Trump's recent remarks at a South Carolina rally have drawn significant criticism for their inflammatory nature. During a campaign event supporting Senator Darline Graham's re-election bid for her late brother's Senate seat, Trump unexpectedly addressed races in Michigan and Texas. His comments targeted Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, stating, 'If you're Black or Jewish and if you vote for Abdul, you're crazy – you're crazy,' adding, 'You're crazy anyway.' item.description: Sarah Matthews, a former deputy press secretary in President Donald Trump's first White House who resigned over the January 6 attack, has criticized Republicans for focusing on a superficial aspect of a recent Barack Obama joke while ignoring its more pointed criticism. During an appearance on CNN's 'The Arena,' Matthews explained that the GOP has latched onto Obama's reference to Trump's White House renovations resembling a Cheesecake Factory, using it to paint Democrats as out-of-touch elitists. However, she argued that the real sting of the joke came from Obama's comparison of Trump to Saddam Hussein, highlighting what she described as Trump's authoritarian behavior and the corruption surrounding his administration and family. item.description: The Justice Department has informed a federal judge that it is 'nearly impossible' to enforce a court order halting tree clearing at a Washington golf course that President Donald Trump aims to renovate. In a motion filed Thursday, government attorneys requested U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes to pause her October 26 injunction while the administration appeals to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit. The motion asks the judge to rule by November 4. Judge Reyes's order prohibits the Interior Department and the National Park Service from cutting additional trees in East Potomac Park, where Trump has pledged to rebuild a public golf course. The government's motion argues that the requirement to notify the court 'without delay' if anyone seeks to alter the park makes compliance 'nearly impossible' and risks sanctions for any failure. item.title: FBI Used Paid Informant to Develop ISIS Plot With Autistic Teen After Dropping Previous Case
item.description: The FBI has been accused of manufacturing an ISIS-inspired attack plot involving an autistic teenager, Abdullah Ezzeldin Taha Mohamed Hassan, by using a paid informant to groom him. According to a motion filed in federal court, the FBI waited until Hassan turned 18 to deploy the informant, three days after his 18th birthday, following the dismissal of a previous case against him. The motion states that the FBI had previously determined Hassan posed no threat when he was 16, and Virginia prosecutors dropped the case in August 2023. The informant, a non-U.S. citizen with a history of felony drug convictions and a pending deportation order, was paid $329,389.18 by the FBI, including $15,000 for the period of the operation. The informant, who was seeking immigration benefits, was instructed to befriend Hassan online and send him FBI-produced propaganda, including a 'CTHS approved bayah video' used to pledge allegiance to ISIS. item.title: Caravan Destroyed in Deliberate Fire on Portland; Two Arrested for Arson
item.description: A caravan was destroyed in a fire that police believe was started deliberately on Yeats Road in Portland, near the Portland Heights Hotel, around 1 a.m. on October 29. Dorset Police responded to the scene to assist the fire service. The incident is being treated as arson, with a 36-year-old woman from Portland and a 34-year-old man from Weymouth arrested on suspicion of arson with intent to endanger life. Both remain in police custody. Detective Sergeant Simon Austin of Dorset County CID emphasized the need for public assistance, urging anyone who witnessed suspicious activity or captured relevant CCTV or dashcam footage to contact authorities. Police have provided contact details for reporting information, including an online portal and the phone number 101, with occurrence number 55260169390. item.description: President Donald Trump engaged in a heated exchange with Reuters White House correspondent Jacob Bogage during an airport press gaggle on Thursday, shortly after canceling a campaign event. The confrontation occurred as Trump was returning to the White House for a Halloween event, following a canceled rally in Rock Hill, South Carolina. Bogage had previously posted an unflattering close-up photo of Trump on X after the president left for the rally. When asked about his health during the brief press gathering, Trump became visibly agitated, calling Bogage 'sick' and 'disgusting' before abruptly ending the session. The president insisted he was 'feeling perfect' and accused the reporter of being 'out of shape' and looking 'like hell.' Trump also criticized Reuters as 'terrible' and dismissed the question about his travel schedule, stating he was 'going to Florida tomorrow' instead of Kansas, where a rally for Senator Roger Marshall had been canceled. item.title: Barbara Barrie, Oscar and Tony-Nominated Actress, Dies at 95 After Advocating for Medical Aid in Dying Law
item.description: Barbara Barrie, an acclaimed actress nominated for both an Academy Award and a Tony Award, has died at the age of 95. Her daughter, Jane Harnick, and her agent confirmed her passing on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, at her Manhattan home. The death was medically assisted following a terminal cancer diagnosis, in compliance with New York State's Medical Aid in Dying Law, a law Barrie had actively supported. Barrie's career spanned over six decades, with notable roles in film, television, and Broadway. She received an Oscar nomination for Best Supporting Actress for her role as Evelyn Stohler in 'Breaking Away' (1979) and an Emmy nomination for the 1980 TV adaptation. Her early career included a Cannes Film Festival Best Actress win for 'One Potato, Two Potato' (1964). On Broadway, she originated the role of Sarah in Stephen Sondheim's 'Company' (1970), earning a Tony nomination. item.title: Democrats grapple with impeachment strategy amid public pressure to hold Trump accountable
item.description: The article examines the growing tension within the Democratic Party regarding impeachment efforts against President Donald Trump in his second term. While over half of American voters believe Trump has committed impeachable offenses, Democratic leaders remain divided on whether to pursue a third impeachment. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has repeatedly stated they 'haven't ruled anything in, and we haven't ruled anything out,' reflecting the party's cautious approach. Several Democrats, including Rep. John Larson and Rep. Shri Thanedar, have introduced impeachment articles against Trump, but most have lost their primaries due to their stance. item.description: David Becker, a former Justice Department attorney and director of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, has criticized President Donald Trump's administration for its attempts to interfere in the upcoming midterm elections. Becker, speaking to Mother Jones, described the administration's efforts as 'a lot of noise' that is failing to achieve its goals. Becker noted that the administration has lost 27 out of 27 lawsuits related to voter data, with nine of those courts presided over by Trump-appointed judges. item.title: Virginia Governor Spanberger's Diverse Cabinet Photo Sparks Conservative Backlash
item.description: Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger (D-VA) faced significant backlash from MAGA influencers after sharing a photo of her cabinet members at the Black History Museum and Cultural Center of Virginia in Richmond. Conservative critics quickly seized on the image, arguing it contained 'too many Black people' to be considered diverse. item.description: Lucy Kate Jackson, born October 29, 1948, is an American actress and television producer who rose to international fame in the mid-1970s as the intelligent and level-headed leader of the original Charlie's Angels. Her career took a significant turn in 1976 when she helped develop and star in ABC's hit series Charlie's Angels, portraying Sabrina Duncan, the smart, grounded, and intuitive leader of the trio alongside Farrah Fawcett and Jaclyn Smith. Jackson played a key role in pitching the show's concept, reportedly suggesting the name 'Charlie's Angels' after seeing a picture of angels in a producer's office. Unlike her co-stars' glamorous and bombshell aesthetics, Jackson stood out for her effortless, tailored sophistication, featuring a signature short brunette shag haircut with soft bangs that became widely copied in the mid-to-late 1970s. item.title: Inflation concerns escalate ahead of midterm elections as PCE index hits 3.6%
item.description: The latest inflation report has intensified economic concerns for President Donald Trump and the Republican Party just days before the midterm elections. According to the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, which is the Federal Reserve's preferred measure of inflation, prices rose at an annual rate of 3.6% in September, marking the highest level since May. This development has sparked warnings from economists and political figures alike. Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, highlighted the worsening inflation trend on social media, stating that "Inflation is back near a 3-year high" and attributing much of the increase to ongoing conflicts in Iran. Representative Ted Lieu (D-CA) quickly seized on the data, criticizing Trump's economic policies as "sucking" and declaring that "The Federal Reserve's preferred measure of inflation (PCE) rose again, this time to 3.6%, the highest since May." item.description: The opening round of the Asia-Pacific Amateur Championship at Te Arai Links' South Course in New Zealand saw Thailand's Pongsapak 'Fifa' Laopakdee take the lead with an eight-under 63, despite challenging wind conditions exceeding 30 mph. The defending champion, who overcame a six-stroke deficit to win in Dubai last year, now aims to become only the second player to win consecutive Asia-Pacific Amateur titles, following Hideki Matsuyama's 2010-2011 victories. Laopakdee's round featured a chip-in eagle on the ninth and nearly holed out on the 15th, showcasing his skill under difficult conditions. Australia's Harry Takis, ranked No. 21 in the World Amateur Golf Ranking, carded a 70 with an eagle on the seventh, leading the field as the highest-ranked player. item.description: Civil society organizations and health workers in Akwa Ibom State, Nigeria, have identified significant barriers preventing vulnerable populations from accessing essential healthcare services for HIV, tuberculosis (TB), and malaria. Despite existing government policies, stigma, cultural restrictions, inadequate health facilities, and confidentiality concerns continue to hinder service uptake. During a one-day meeting in Uyo, stakeholders emphasized the need for urgent government action to improve accessibility for women and other marginalized groups. Key recommendations included enhancing public awareness of available services, training health workers to provide non-discriminatory care, and equipping primary healthcare centers to better serve communities. Participants also stressed the importance of consistent data collection to track disease cases and assess policy implementation. item.title: Patrick Stewart, Iconic 'Star Trek' and 'X-Men' Actor, Passes Away at 86
item.description: Patrick Stewart, the renowned actor celebrated for his iconic roles as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in 'Star Trek: The Next Generation' and Professor Charles Xavier in the 'X-Men' film series, has died at the age of 86. According to a statement from his longtime spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak, Stewart passed away at his Los Angeles home following a brief but poignant battle with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia. The statement described his final moments as filled with family, friends, live music, prayer, tears, and laughter, reflecting the profound impact he had on those around him throughout his career. Stewart's career began in British theater, with decades of classical work before he gained international fame in the late 1980s. item.description: The Justice Department under President Donald Trump is opposing efforts to consolidate two lawsuits filed by Jeffrey Epstein survivors who claim the FBI failed to act on their reports. item.title: Trump's Antisemitism Task Force Leader Threatened to Choke Jewish Intern, Harvard Report Reveals

According to the report, Terrell threatened to choke a Jewish intern with a computer charger, isolated Jewish interns, berated them, and repeatedly threatened their jobs or careers. item.title: Rally attendee compares Trump event to Jonestown Massacre during Fox News interview

item.description: President Donald Trump appeared to be confused when asked about the firing of the Pentagon's top military planner, Lt. Gen. item.description: Miles Taylor, former chief of staff at the Department of Homeland Security under President Trump, has written in his DEFIANCE.org newsletter that former President Barack Obama's joke about Cheesecake Factory 'baited' Trump into making a self-defeating political move days before the midterms. item.title: Ohio restaurant owner and Trump supporter Adam Radogna charged with possessing child sexual abuse material
item.description: Adam Radogna, a 37-year-old restaurant owner from Brook Park, Ohio, and a prominent supporter of former President Donald Trump, has been indicted on 10 felony charges related to the alleged possession of child sexual abuse material. According to reports from WEWS-TV, a Cuyahoga County grand jury issued the indictment on Wednesday. item.description: A recent study conducted by researchers at Tongji University in China has revealed that breaking resistance training into short, frequent sessions throughout the day can produce strength and endurance gains similar to those achieved through a single, continuous workout. The eight-week experiment involved 45 young male participants aged 18 to 25 who regularly lifted weights. Participants were divided into two groups: one performing three 1-minute sessions of 20 weighted squats each (totaling 60 squats), and the other completing a single 60-squat session. Both groups used a Smith machine under expert supervision, with weights progressively increased over time. item.title: Neural Mechanisms Link Reinforcement Learning to Motor Efficiency in Aplysia Feeding Circuit
item.description: A groundbreaking study published in Communications Biology has uncovered how reinforcement learning shapes both the selection of motor actions and the timing of their execution in the Aplysia feeding circuit. Researchers led by Yuto Momohara, Curtis L. Neveu, and John H. Byrne from the University of Texas Health Science Center conducted experiments using an ex vivo operant conditioning paradigm on the Aplysia feeding circuit. Their findings reveal that reinforcement biases motor program selection toward ingestive behaviors while simultaneously shortening the duration of these actions by advancing the transition from protraction to retraction phases in feeding movements. The study identified specific neural mechanisms underlying this temporal compression, demonstrating that operant conditioning reduces the intrinsic electrical excitability of neuron B52, which weakens B52-mediated inhibition of the retraction-initiating interneuron B64. item.description: The Washington Post article 'How to stop a 'what if' anxiety spiral before it takes over' by Anna Borges discusses the common experience of anxiety spirals that begin with a single worry and escalate into catastrophic thinking. The author explains how a simple concern, such as a date going poorly, a work mistake, or an unusual medical test result, can quickly spiral into overwhelming 'what if' scenarios like 'What if I never find someone?' or 'What if I'm dying?'. The article provides four practical strategies from a psychologist to interrupt this worst-case thinking pattern. These include recognizing the spiral early, challenging the validity of catastrophic thoughts, grounding oneself in the present moment, and developing a structured plan for potential outcomes. The piece emphasizes that while anxiety is a natural response, it becomes problematic when it leads to persistent negative thinking that impacts daily functioning. item.title: Francis Halzen Awarded Nobel Prize in Physics 2026 for IceCube Neutrino Observatory Contributions
item.description: The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced on October 6 that Belgian-American physicist and astrophysicist Francis Halzen has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for his decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos. This marks the first unshared Physics Nobel since 1992 and the fifth in history related to neutrinos. Halzen's work bridges particle physics and astrophysics, focusing on the detection of neutrinos, often called 'ghost particles' due to their near-invisibility and ability to pass through matter without interaction. The article details the historical context of neutrino research, from Wolfgang Pauli's 1931 theoretical prediction to the 1956 experimental confirmation by Clyde Cowan and Frederick Reines. item.description: The article, written by Ray Richmond, a journalist and adjunct professor, argues that the upcoming midterm elections will serve as a referendum on Donald Trump's presidency and his ongoing legal and political controversies. item.title: Daily Fiber Supplement Shows Promise in Reducing Knee Arthritis Pain and Enhancing Muscle Strength
item.description: A clinical trial led by researchers at the University of Nottingham has revealed that a daily prebiotic fiber supplement, specifically inulin, can significantly reduce knee osteoarthritis (OA) pain while improving muscle strength. The study, published in the journal Nutrients, involved 117 adults with knee OA who were assigned to one of four treatment groups: inulin alone, digital physical therapy exercises (PSE) alone, a combination of inulin and PSE, or a placebo. Participants taking inulin experienced notable pain reduction, improved grip strength, and decreased pain sensitivity compared to those in the physical therapy group. The supplement also demonstrated a much higher adherence rate, with only 3.6% dropout in the inulin group versus 21% in the physical therapy group. Inulin, a naturally occurring fiber found in foods like chicory root and Jerusalem artichokes, is not broken down by digestive enzymes but instead nourishes beneficial gut bacteria in the large intestine. item.title: Critical UEFI Firmware Flaw Affects Most Servers, Allows Pre-Boot Code Execution
item.description: A critical vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-97631, has been discovered in the TianoCore EDK II open-source codebase used by most server vendors and data centers for UEFI firmware. The flaw, rated 9.5 out of 10 in severity, is a memory-corruption issue in the ICMP component that allows attackers to execute malicious code before the operating system and firmware defenses like Secure Boot activate. The vulnerability affects the PXE-Base Code driver (NetworkPkg/UefiPxeBcDxe), which handles network boot processes, enabling attackers to send malicious ICMP error messages that overwrite memory buffers. This can lead to code execution in ring 0, the most privileged CPU level, before security mechanisms like TPM and Secure Boot are engaged. The flaw has been present for 16 years and impacts systems that boot from network resources, including servers, storage equipment, and devices relying on EDK2-based firmware. Mobile teams frequently change locations, with residents warning each other through local Telegram groups. Social media and news outlets have documented cases of beatings, unlawful detentions, and denial of access to lawyers. The Ukrainian ombudsman has reported a significant increase in complaints about these practices, with some cases leading to criminal convictions. However, many convictions result in suspended sentences, allowing offenders to continue serving. item.title: Sauna Bathing Temporarily Boosts Immune Cell Circulation, Study Finds
item.description: A recent study conducted by researchers in Finland has revealed that a single 30-minute sauna session, followed by a brief cold shower, triggers a temporary surge in white blood cells circulating in the bloodstream. The findings, published in the journal Temperature, indicate that sauna bathing mobilizes immune cells that typically reside in tissues, allowing them to move more freely throughout the body. This increased circulation enhances the body's ability to monitor for pathogens such as bacteria and viruses. The study measured various types of white blood cells, including neutrophils and lymphocytes, which are critical for immune responses. Neutrophils act as first responders to infections, while lymphocytes are involved in recognizing specific threats and producing antibodies. The increase in these cells was observed immediately after the sauna session but returned to baseline levels within 30 minutes. item.title: Faith Domergue: A 1950s Horror and Sci-Fi Star Known for Her Dark Beauty
item.description: Faith Domergue (1924 or 1925–1999) was an American actress celebrated for her dark beauty and significant roles in 1950s science fiction and horror films. Discovered as a teenager by Howard Hughes, she was signed to a contract and groomed for stardom, though her early career faced delays and limited opportunities. Domergue gained lasting recognition in the mid-1950s with appearances in cult classics such as This Island Earth (1955), It Came from Beneath the Sea (1955), and Cult of the Cobra (1955), earning her a place among the era’s early 'scream queens.' Her striking features and intense screen presence made her a distinctive figure in mid-century genre cinema. item.description: In April 2025, Samsung introduced Vision AI sets with features called Pet Care and Family Care, which could detect dog barks or baby cries in an empty room and send alerts to owners' phones. The company stated these features only worked when the TV was turned off. However, on October 23, 2026, a reverse engineer known as log4j shared findings suggesting Samsung TVs send data about barks, cries, sensor readings, and camera streaming duration to Samsung servers. The researcher discovered this through unpatched security flaws that allowed full control of the TV, revealing sound-classification models, screen capture logs, and cross-device advertising IDs. Samsung's automatic content recognition (ACR) system, which samples screen content twice per second, has been documented for years, but the new claims involve potential audio data collection. The researcher alleges that even when ACR is turned off, data might still be transmitted. Samsung has disputed the claims, stating that viewing-reco

item.title: GOP Strategist Criticizes Ex-Trump Aide's Proposal to Cut Ukraine Funding to End War
item.description: On Wednesday's episode of CNN's 'NewsNight,' guest-hosted by Michael Smerconish, Republican strategist Shermichael Singleton engaged in a heated exchange with Caroline Sunshine, a former Trump White House aide, over her proposal to end the Ukraine-Russia conflict by cutting U.S. funding to Ukraine. Sunshine argued that the U.S. should withdraw financial support to force Ukraine to negotiate a peace deal, stating that Ukraine is not a NATO ally and the U.S. has no role in the war except to end it. Singleton strongly opposed the idea, calling it 'the most absurd thing' and accusing Sunshine of being 'incredibly naive.' He emphasized that Russia, not Ukraine, initiated the conflict, noting that 'it wasn't the Ukrainians. It was the Russians.' Singleton further criticized Sunshine for suggesting that Ukraine should be pressured to negotiate, arguing that the U.S. has never taken such a stance before. item.title: Vali Myers: Australian Artist and Spiritual Pioneer of Positano
item.description: Vali Myers, widely known as the 'Witch of Positano,' was an Australian artist, dancer, and mystic whose life spanned the post-war avant-garde scenes of Paris, New York's Chelsea Hotel, and a remote Italian canyon. Born in Sydney in 1930, Myers became a prominent figure in the Beatnik movement in Paris, where she was photographed by Ed van der Elsken for his book 'Love on the Left Bank.' She associated with cultural icons like Jean Cocteau, Allen Ginsberg, and Jean-Paul Sartre. After overcoming an opium addiction, Myers retreated with her partner Rudi Rappold to a cliffside ravine near Positano, Italy, where they lived in an abandoned stone structure without modern amenities. For decades, she immersed herself in nature, creating intricate pen-and-ink and watercolor drawings that depicted mystical themes, animal forms, and powerful representations of femininity. She also established a wildlife sanctuary for rescued animals, contributing to the area's protection as a WWF oasis. Myers main

item.title: Bluesky Blocks Links to DHS Employee Data Leak, Citing Safety Concerns
item.description: Bluesky has blocked links to a newly leaked archive containing records of over 41,000 Department of Homeland Security (DHS) employees and contractors, labeling the pages as 'malicious.' The files include personal contact information such as email addresses and phone numbers, shared without authorization, which violates Bluesky's community guidelines. The company chose to block the links rather than remove individual posts to avoid restricting public discussion or broader access to reporting on the leak. The DHS records, published by the transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets), detail employee names, contact information, and internal group memberships, including those tied to surveillance and undercover operations. A WIRED investigation revealed the files provide insight into DHS organizational structure, from leadership to individual immigration agents, and who has access to certain technologies. item.title: Snow Peak Campfield: A Japanese-Inspired Retreat on Washington's Long Beach Peninsula
item.description: Snow Peak Campfield, located on Washington's Long Beach Peninsula, offers a unique blend of Japanese design and Pacific Northwest natural beauty. The campfield features Jyubako suites, small cabins made of pale pine and plywood, each approximately 200 square feet with a queen bed, futon, kitchenette, and private bathroom. Priced from $130 per night, these cabins are designed to encourage guests to stay connected with nature, with low furniture that positions the eye at the top edge of the glass door to the porch, gently nudging guests outside. The main attraction is the Ofuro, a Japanese-style bathhouse with a hot pool maintained at 104 degrees, a hinoki cypress sauna, cold plunge, and showers. The bathhouse is thoughtfully designed with angled beams echoing the surrounding trees and an open side facing a grove of alders at the edge of a pond. The Long Beach Peninsula, where the campfield is situated, is known for its wide sandy beaches, razor clamming, kite flying, and storm watching.

item.title: MUHC Researchers Identify New Vesicles Linked to Cancer Cell Migration and Metastasis
item.description: Researchers at McGill University Health Centre (MUHC) have identified a novel mechanism by which migrating cancer cells communicate and spread throughout the body. The study, led by Prof. Julia Burnier and PhD student Thupten Tsering, reveals that cancer cells release specialized structures called motile vesicles (MoVes), which carry genetic material including cancer-associated mutations. These vesicles, previously thought to be cellular waste, are now understood to play a critical role in cell-to-cell communication during cancer progression. The discovery emerged unexpectedly while investigating how cancer cells release DNA, leading to the identification of MoVes as a key component in the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) process. EMT is a biological mechanism that allows cells to become more mobile and invasive, contributing to tumor progression and treatment resistance. item.title: Early Voting by Black Voters Rises in Southern States Ahead of 2026 Midterms
item.description:
Early voting among Black Americans has increased significantly ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, particularly in Southern states where Republican redistricting efforts have targeted majority-Black congressional districts. According to The Bulwark, Black voters have cast more than 160,000 additional ballots compared with the same stage of the 2022 midterm elections, raising questions about whether Republican efforts to reshape electoral districts could have unintended political consequences.
The developments follow the Supreme Court's ruling in Louisiana v. Callais, a case that originated in Louisiana and weakened the protections provided by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act. Following the decision, Republicans in several states moved to redraw congressional maps and dismantle majority-Black districts. item.title: Trump Administration Challenges Court Order on Park Closure for Golf Course Renovation
item.description: The Trump administration's Justice Department has raised objections to a federal court order requiring detailed notice before closing East Potomac Park in Washington, D.C., for a golf course renovation. In a filing with the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, the department argued that the court's requirements for 'prompt notice' and extensive documentation, including naming every individual involved and assessing the impact on the park, are overly burdensome. The closure, scheduled for November 15, is part of a plan to replace the current public golf course with a 'World Class, championship-level golf course' designed by Tom Fazio, capable of hosting major tournaments like the U.S. Open and the Ryder Cup. The National Park Service has signed a new lease with National Links Trust, the company currently operating the East Potomac Golf Course, which will cease operations by the closure date but will continue managing Rock Creek and Langston golf courses. item.title: Dancing With the Stars Season 35 Features First Perfect Score and Double Elimination During Horror Movie-Themed Episode
item.description: Dancing With the Stars season 35 celebrated Halloween with a horror movie-themed episode, featuring performances inspired by films such as Saw, Black Swan, and Joker. The episode marked the first perfect score of the season when Harry Shum Jr. and Jenna Johnson earned a 40/40 for their contemporary dance to 'Toxic' by 2WEI, inspired by the horror film Saw. This performance placed them at the top of the leaderboard with a combined score of 76/80 after combining scores from both Horror Movie Night and Dedication Night. The episode also saw the elimination of two couples: Jackson Olson and Emma Slater, and Tyler Cameron and Sharna Burgess, who had the lowest combined scores. The elimination was determined by a combination of judges' scores and viewer votes from both Dedication and Horror Movie Night. item.title: Europe moves toward direct talks with Russia amid shifting geopolitical dynamics
item.description: After months of hesitation and internal debate, European leaders are signaling a decisive shift toward direct engagement with Russia to address the Ukraine conflict and reshape continental security architecture. Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre recently held a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, marking a significant step in Europe's diplomatic approach. While lacking formal mandates, their initiative positioned Nordic leaders as key interlocutors, with the Kremlin confirming plans for continued direct communication. The European Commission and Council are preparing a joint delegation, led by Bjoern Seibert, to join upcoming talks in Abu Dhabi, aiming for a multilateral format involving Europeans, Ukrainians, Americans, and Russians—a departure from previous US-centric negotiations. item.title: Defense Secretary Hegseth removes Pentagon chief planner amid strategic uncertainty
item.description: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has removed Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, the Pentagon's chief planner, from his position on the Joint Chiefs of Staff without providing an explanation, according to The Atlantic. Sylvia, who led the Joint Staff's strategy, plans and policy directorate (J5), is the second person to be removed from that role within a year, following the forced retirement of his predecessor, Army Lt. Gen. Joseph McGee. The timing of the removal is particularly sensitive as President Donald Trump considers potential military action against Iran following next week's elections, with U.S. Central Command reportedly preparing strike options ranging from limited strikes on nuclear sites to broader economic pressure campaigns. A former Joint Chiefs of Staff official described the J5 role as a critical bridge between field troops, Pentagon policy, and the White House, suggesting that losing this position at this moment could be problematic. item.title: Measles Outbreak Spreads from South Carolina to Washington State in Multiple Incidents
item.description: The news article details multiple instances of measles transmission from South Carolina to Washington state within a two-week period. According to the report, there were five distinct importation events where individuals from South Carolina traveled to Washington state and subsequently spread the virus. In the first incident, South Carolina residents visited public places while infectious, leading to four residents with close contact falling ill. These four individuals then visited schools, healthcare facilities, and a church, causing nine additional cases among their contacts and one person exposed in a public location, totaling 14 cases from January 15 to February 17. The second incident involved two state residents returning from South Carolina who fell ill on January 15-16, but no additional cases were linked to them. item.description: A prominent economist, Justin Wolfers, has expressed confusion over Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh's decision to maintain current interest rates instead of implementing a rate hike that markets anticipate. In his Platypus Economics newsletter, Wolfers noted that the Fed's decision to hold rates steady on Wednesday appears to be a six-week delay of an expected move, with markets already pricing in an 80% chance of a hike at the December meeting. Wolfers argued that the Fed's preferred inflation measure remains at 3.4% year-over-year through August, while consumer prices rose 3.7% through September, indicating that the economy still requires monetary tightening. item.description: Britt McHenry, a former press advisor for the State Department and a former ESPN host, has publicly addressed the incident at a Washington Wizards basketball game that resulted in her losing her position. In a video posted on X, McHenry explained that she threw her beer at a group of hecklers after one of them made a derogatory comment about her 'getting gang raped outside.' The event, part of his 'Come and Take It Tour,' was held at the Arc Light Bar & Grill inside a Clarion Hotel. The space was set up with only two rows of stadium chairs, and a Facebook video showed Paxton speaking for approximately 15 minutes. The Daily Beast reported that the campaign did not respond to inquiries about why the larger ballroom was not used. item.title: Trump's White House staff reports growing instability amid midterm election concerns
item.description: According to a New York Times report, President Donald Trump's behavior has become increasingly erratic behind closed doors, causing concern among those closest to him. The report, based on interviews with 16 current and former administration officials and Trump allies, reveals a sense of gloom descending on the White House less than a week before Election Day. Trump has been shrinking his circle of confidants, lashing out at critics, and dismissing polls showing his unpopularity. Many Republicans in competitive races are distancing themselves from the president, with some GOP advisers privately warning that his battleground rallies may harm rather than help their campaigns. Trump, however, remains determined to make the midterms a referendum on himself.
